report:
## What the evidence shows

There's real science behind this claim, but it's more nuanced than a blanket "yes."

**The core mechanism: CO2 buildup.** Multiple controlled studies (Strøm-Tejsen et al., published in *Indoor Air*, and a 2023 DTU-led field study) show that closed bedrooms accumulate exhaled CO2 overnight, often exceeding 1,000–2,600 ppm. Higher CO2 correlates with reduced sleep efficiency, more awakenings, less deep sleep, and worse next-day concentration, sleepiness, and logical-thinking performance. Ventilating with an open window or door keeps CO2 below roughly 750–1,000 ppm and is associated with measurably better objective and subjective sleep and next-day cognitive performance (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168, dtu.dk, mdpi.com/2075-5309/13/11/2768, sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132323011459).

**But context matters.** A Shanghai field study found that although opening windows improved bedroom air quality, actual sleep quality did not improve overall in summer, because open windows also let in more heat and outdoor noise—both independent sleep disruptors (sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed). Similarly, in areas with poor outdoor air quality, heavy pollution, allergens, or traffic noise, opening a window can offset or reverse any ventilation benefit (molekule.com/en-ca/blogs/all/sleep-window-open-night).

## Bottom line

Your sister's claim has solid supporting evidence when the goal is specifically reducing CO2/stuffiness—lower CO2 does correlate with better sleep and alertness in lab and field studies. However, "opening a window improves sleep" isn't universally true: benefits depend on outdoor air quality, noise, temperature, and season. It's a reasonable general practice in clean, quiet, temperate conditions, but not a guaranteed fix everywhere.
